title: Nouns, Gender, and the Verb Būti
summary: Every noun is masculine or feminine and announces which by its ending; there is no article; the verb *būti* joins a subject to a predicate noun or adjective, and the adjective agrees in gender.

rules.heading: Gender
rules.statement: Every Lithuanian noun is either **masculine** or **feminine**. There is no neuter. Gender is not a statement about the thing named — a table is masculine and a book feminine for no reason outside the grammar — but it governs the form of every adjective, pronoun and participle that refers to the noun, and so must be known for each word. Fortunately the ending usually declares it.

rules.heading: The Endings of the Nominative Singular
rules.statement: In the form under which a noun is listed in the dictionary, masculine nouns end in **-as, -is, -ys** or **-us**, and feminine nouns in **-a** or **-ė**. The ending is thus a nearly reliable guide to gender. The one trap is **-is**, which belongs chiefly to masculines but also to a small closed class of feminines, of which *moteris*, woman, is the commonest.

paradigms.caption: Nominative singular endings
paradigms.footnote: Feminine in -is: moteris (woman), akis (eye), naktis (night), širdis (heart). These must be learned individually.

rules.heading: Absence of the Article
rules.statement: Lithuanian has **neither a definite nor an indefinite article**. *Namas* is at once "a house" and "the house", and which is meant is settled by the context, or, where it matters, by a demonstrative such as *tas*, that. The beginner whose own language has articles must resist the urge to supply one.

rules.heading: The Nominative Case
rules.statement: Lithuanian nouns are declined in **seven cases**, of which the first is the **nominative**. The nominative is the form given in dictionaries, and it is used for the **subject** of the sentence — the person or thing of which something is asserted. The remaining cases are taken up in the lessons that follow.

rules.heading: The Personal Pronouns
rules.statement: The personal pronouns in the nominative are given below. The third person distinguishes gender, there being a masculine and a feminine form in both numbers. Because the verb ending already shows the person, the pronoun is commonly **omitted** unless it is emphatic or needed to make clear which of two persons is meant.

paradigms.caption: Personal pronouns, nominative

rows.label: 2nd person
cells: jūs — you (more than one, or polite)

paradigms.footnote: *jie* is used of a mixed company; *jos* only where every member is feminine.

examples.note: the pronoun dropped; the ending -u says 'I' already

rules.heading: The Present Tense of Būti
rules.statement: The verb **būti**, to be, is irregular and must be learned entire. Note that the third person has **one form for both numbers and all genders** — a feature of every Lithuanian verb, not of this one alone.

paradigms.caption: būti — present tense
paradigms.footnote: Negated by prefixing ne-: nesu, nesi, nesame, nesate. The third person is irregular: **nėra**, not *neyra*.

rules.heading: The Predicate Noun and Adjective
rules.statement: When a noun or adjective is joined to the subject by *būti* and forms part of what is asserted of it, it is called a **predicate noun** or **predicate adjective**. Such a word stands in the **nominative**, exactly like the subject, because it names the subject rather than being acted upon by it.

rules.heading: Agreement of the Adjective
rules.statement: An adjective **agrees with its noun in gender**, whether it stands before the noun as an attribute or after *būti* as a predicate. Adjectives fall into three classes by their endings: **-as / -a**, **-us / -i**, and **-is / -ė**. Choosing the wrong class is the commonest error at this stage; the masculine form given in the vocabulary settles which class a given adjective belongs to.

examples.note: katė is feminine, so maža and not mažas

footnotes: An attributive adjective normally precedes its noun, as in English.

rules.heading: Word Order
rules.statement: Because the endings show what each word is doing, word order is **freer than in English** and is used for emphasis rather than for grammar. The ordinary, unemphatic order is nevertheless subject – verb – predicate, and the learner should keep to it until the effect of departing from it is understood.

examples.note: emphatic; the same words, a different point

vocabulary.notes: Feminine although it ends in -is. Compare akis (eye), naktis (night), širdis (heart).

drills.explanation: The ending -a marks a feminine noun. -as and -is here mark masculines.

drills.stem: How many genders does Lithuanian distinguish?
drills.explanation: Two, masculine and feminine. Unlike Latin, German or Russian, Lithuanian has no neuter noun.
*knyga* is feminine, so the predicate adjective takes the feminine -a. *esu* is the first person, and *nėra* negates.
*mes esame*, we are. *esate* belongs to jūs, *esu* to aš, and *yra* serves the whole third person.
*katė* and *mergaitė* are feminine and *namas* and *brolis* masculine; the adjective must follow suit. *Katė yra maža* and *Brolis yra naujas* would be right.

drills.stem: *Namas yra didelis* can mean both "a house is big" and "the house is big". Why?
options: Because the nominative case is ambiguous between the two.
Because Lithuanian has no articles, definite or indefinite.
Because the adjective follows the noun.
drills.explanation: There is no word for "a" or "the". Definiteness is left to the context, or shown by a demonstrative where it matters.
-as and -is mark masculines here; -ė and -a mark feminines.

drills.stem: *Moteris*, woman, ends in -is, yet takes feminine adjectives. What does this show?
options: That -is nouns are feminine and -as nouns masculine.
That gender in Lithuanian follows the meaning of the word.
That the ending -is is mostly masculine but has a small feminine class, so gender must be learned with the word.
drills.explanation: Endings are a good guide, not a law. -is is chiefly masculine, but a closed set — moteris, akis, naktis, širdis — is feminine and must be memorised.

drills.stem: In the sentence **Mokytoja yra gera**, how many words stand in the nominative case?
drills.explanation: Two: the subject *mokytoja* and the predicate adjective *gera*, which takes the nominative because it names the subject rather than being acted upon. *yra* is a verb and has no case.

drills.title: Namas
drills.passage: Tai namas. Namas yra didelis ir naujas. Čia yra Jonas. Jonas yra mokytojas. Jis yra geras mokytojas. Čia yra Rūta. Rūta yra mokytoja. Ji yra graži. Namas yra mokykla.
drills.translation: This is a house. The house is big and new. Here is Jonas. Jonas is a teacher. He is a good teacher. Here is Rūta. Rūta is a teacher. She is beautiful. The house is a school.

questions.explanation: *Jonas yra mokytojas* — the masculine form. *mokytoja* would be a woman.

questions.stem: Which statements does the passage make about **namas**?
questions.explanation: The passage calls the house big, new, and a school. *Namas yra maža* is doubly wrong: the passage does not say it, and *maža* is feminine where *mažas* would be required.

questions.stem: How many people are named in the passage?
questions.explanation: Two: Jonas, referred to afterwards as *jis*, and Rūta, referred to as *ji*.
